name: Judgment Sunday / Christ the King Day
description: The last Sunday of the church year. The return of Christ and the final judgment.
biblicalBasis: The parable of the sheep and the goats: 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, take your inheritance, the kingdom prepared for you... Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me' (Matt 25:31-46). Daniel's vision of the Son of Man: 'One like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven... He was given authority, glory and sovereign power' (Dan 7:13-14). Revelation 21:1-5 about the new heaven and the new earth: 'Behold, I am making all things new.'
significance: The church year ends with a look forward — Christ returning as judge and king. The judgment in Matt 25 is surprisingly concrete: it is actions toward 'the least' that decide. Christ's kingship is not a distant future event — it is a present reality to be fulfilled. History has a goal: God's kingdom will be completed.
liturgicalContext: White or green color. The last Sunday of the church year — next Sunday is the first Sunday of Advent and a new church year begins. The circle closes: from waiting (Advent) through birth, death, resurrection and the work of the Spirit to judgment and completion.
history: Christ the King Day was introduced in the Catholic Church by Pius XI in 1925, but the theme of judgment and return on the last Sunday of the church year is much older in Protestant tradition. Luther emphasized Christ's kingship as a comfort for believers and a warning to oppressors.
otConnections: Daniel 7:13-14 about the Son of Man as the key text. Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 about the new heaven and the new earth. Zechariah 14:9: 'The Lord will be king over the whole earth.' Psalms 96 and 98 about the Lord coming to judge the earth. Isaiah 11:1-9 about the kingdom of peace where the wolf lives with the lamb.

references.reason: The text about those who are persecuted (vv. 10-12) and the strict ethical demands leading to the final judgment (vv. 21-48: 'guilty before the judge', 'hellfire', 'be perfect as your Father is perfect') are directly relevant to Judgment Sunday's theme of the final judgment and Christ's return.

The day concerns the final judgment and Christ's kingdom. The whole chapter (Matt 6) provides an ethical preparation for judgment: where have we placed our trust (treasures on earth vs. in heaven), whom do we serve (God or Mammon), and how do we live trusting the Father until the day of judgment?

Verse 15 contains a direct reference to 'the day of judgment' and compares the judgment on a city that does not receive the disciples with the judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah. This is a central theme for Judgment Sunday (Christ the King Day), which focuses on the final judgment and Christ's return.

Verses 22-23 link persecution and endurance to 'the Son of Man coming'. This is a prophecy about Jesus' return, which is the main theme of Judgment Sunday. The text emphasizes that history has a goal and that faith must endure until the end.
Verses 32-33 deal with Jesus' role as judge by confessing or denying people before the Father on the day of judgment. This is a direct connection to the reality of judgment celebrated on this day.

Verses 40-42 describe how actions toward 'the least' (the disciples) are counted as actions toward Jesus himself, and that this determines the reward. This mirrors the parable of the sheep and the goats (Matt 25), which is the main text for Judgment Sunday, where judgment is based on concrete action toward the weak.

The verses contain a direct warning about the day of judgment (36-37) and comparisons with Nineveh and the queen of the South who will stand in judgment (41-42). This strongly connects to Judgment Sunday's theme, even though the text is primarily read during Lent.
The parable of the weeds deals centrally with the final judgment and separation at the end of the world, a main theme for Judgment Sunday.
Jesus' explanation of the weeds describes the mechanism of judgment (angels, furnace of fire, separation), which is central to Judgment Sunday.
The parable of the net describes the final judgment and separation between the good and the bad, a central theme for Judgment Sunday.

Matt 16:24-28 deals with the Son of Man coming in his Father's glory to 'reward each person according to what they have done' (v. 27). This is a direct reference to the final judgment and Christ's return. Verses 24-26 set the premises for judgment by defining discipleship as a path through suffering, which is central to the message of Judgment Sunday.

The day concerns Christ's return and the final judgment. The text contains strong eschatological warnings about 'eternal fire' and 'hellfire' (vv. 8-9) as well as the promise that the Father does not want any of these little ones to be lost (v. 14). This gives a concrete picture of who will be judged and who will be saved, which is relevant for Judgment Sunday's theology.

The whole chapter builds up to Jesus' revelation about the final judgment and the logic of God's kingdom. The theme 'the first will be last' (v. 30) and the Son of Man as judge (v. 28) are central to the entire text, not just the end. The chapter deals with what is required to enter God's kingdom (eternal life), and the conclusion with judgment over the tribes of Israel is the climax of this discussion.

The parable of the wedding feast (Matt 22:1-14) is one of the most central texts for Judgment Sunday. It deals with God's call, humanity's response, the final judgment on those who reject the call, and the separation between the 'called' and the 'chosen'. The king's actions illustrate Christ's role as judge at the end of the world.

The question about paying taxes (vv. 15-22) and the debate with the Sadducees about resurrection (vv. 23-33) deal with God's sovereignty over the state and life after death. These themes are central to Judgment Sunday (Christ the King Day and the final judgment), even though the events historically take place during Holy Week.

The question about the greatest commandment (vv. 34-40) and the question about the Messiah's identity (vv. 41-46) confirm Jesus' divine status and his position at God's right hand. This underscores that Jesus is the one who will come as judge and king, a central theme for Judgment Sunday.

The chapter is dominated by seven 'Woe to you' statements expressing God's judgment on hypocrisy and rejection of prophets. The text deals with the final judgment (Gehenna), shutting the kingdom of heaven, and that a generation will have all righteous blood come upon them. This is one of the most central texts for Judgment Sunday (Christ the King Day), where the focus is on Christ's judgment and the end of history.

The whole of Matthew 24 is the central text for Judgment Sunday (Christ the King Day). The chapter describes the coming of the Son of Man on the clouds of heaven with power and glory (v. 30), the gathering of the elect (v. 31), the parables about being awake and ready (vv. 32-51), and the final judgment. This is the main theme of the day, and the whole chapter should be marked as primary.

This is the main text for Judgment Sunday (Christ the King Day). The parable of the sheep and the goats (vv. 31-46) is the central text describing the final judgment at Christ's return, which is the theme of this day. The text is explicitly mentioned in today's description.

The parable of the ten virgins (vv. 1-13) is part of the same chapter and deals with being ready for the Lord's coming. It is often used as a preparatory text to the parable of the sheep and the goats on Judgment Sunday, focusing on 'watching' and not knowing the day or hour (v. 13).

The parable of the talents (vv. 14-30) is also part of Matthew 25 and deals with responsibility and faithfulness during the waiting time before the Lord comes to settle accounts. It is often read in connection with Judgment Sunday or during Lent as an exhortation to use God's gifts, but it is not the main text for Judgment Sunday in the same way as the sheep and the goats.
